items.stem: All 20 standard amino acids share a central (alpha) carbon covalently bonded to which set of groups?

choices.text: A hydroxyl group, a carboxyl group, and two R groups
An amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group
Two carboxyl groups, a hydrogen atom, and an R group
An amino group, a phosphate group, a hydrogen atom, and an R group

items.explanation: The alpha carbon of every standard amino acid is bonded to an amino group (-NH2/-NH3+), a carboxyl group (-COOH/-COO-), a hydrogen atom, and a distinguishing side chain (R). Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified. OpenStax Biology 2e ch.3 (Biological Macromolecules: Proteins) https://openstax.org/details/books/biology-2e

items.stem: A neutral amino acid such as glycine (side-chain has no ionizable group) exists predominantly as a zwitterion at physiological pH. Its isoelectric point (pI) is best calculated as:

choices.text: The pKa of the carboxyl group alone
The average of the pKa of the carboxyl group and the pKa of the amino group
Always exactly 7.0 regardless of the amino acid
The pKa of the amino group alone

items.explanation: For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the net charge is zero midway between its two relevant pKa values, so pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2, the average of the alpha-carboxyl (~2) and alpha-amino (~9-10) pKa values, giving a pI near 6. Using only the carboxyl pKa or only the amino pKa ignores the other ionizable group, and the pI is not a fixed 7.0 because it depends on the specific pKa values of each amino acid. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified. OpenStax Chemistry 2e (acid-base behavior of amino acids) https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e

items.stem: The peptide bond shows restricted rotation and is essentially planar. The best explanation is that:

choices.text: Resonance gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character
Hydrogen bonding freezes the bond in place
The bond is a true carbon-carbon double bond

items.explanation: Delocalization of the carbonyl electrons gives the peptide (C-N) bond partial double-bond character, which prevents free rotation and holds the six atoms of the peptide group in a plane (usually the trans configuration). The peptide bond is not a true carbon-carbon double bond, and although hydrogen bonds and disulfide bridges stabilize higher-order structure, neither is the cause of peptide-bond planarity. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified. LibreTexts Biochemistry: Fundamentals of Biochemistry (Jakubowski & Flatt), Protein Structure https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Biochemistry/Fundamentals_of_Biochemistry_(Jakubowski_and_Flatt)

items.stem: Apoptosis is best described as:

choices.text: Programmed, controlled cell death that is a normal part of development and tissue maintenance

items.stem: Action potentials obey the 'all-or-none' principle, which means that:

choices.text: Once threshold is reached, an action potential of full amplitude fires; below threshold, none fires
Every stimulus, no matter how small, triggers an action potential
Action potentials gradually fade as the stimulus weakens
A stronger stimulus produces a larger-amplitude action potential

items.explanation: If a stimulus depolarizes the membrane to threshold, a complete action potential fires at full magnitude; if it fails to reach threshold, no action potential occurs. items.stem: During the absolute refractory period, a neuron cannot fire another action potential no matter how strong the stimulus. The main reason is that:

choices.text: The Na+/K+ pump has stopped working
The neuron has run out of neurotransmitter
Voltage-gated Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes

items.explanation: In the absolute refractory period, the voltage-gated Na+ channels are in an inactivated state and cannot be reopened until the membrane repolarizes, so no new action potential can occur; this also ensures the impulse travels in one direction. items.stem: A social movement arises when people feel deprived relative to others or to their own expectations, even if they are not the worst off in absolute terms. This explanation is:

items.stem: A ball is released from rest and falls freely for 3.0 s (g = 10 m/s², neglect air resistance). What is its speed just before landing? Give the value with units.

choices.text: Newton's second law: F_net = m a = (2.0 kg)(3.0 m/s²) = 6.0 N.

items.explanation: From rest v₀ = 0, so speed grows linearly as v = g t. The distance fallen (½ g t² = 45 m) is a common trap; it is a length, not a speed. passages.title: psg-bb-1
passages.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

questions.stem: Based on its effect on the kinetic parameters, Inhibitor A is best classified as which type of inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Inhibitor A leaves Vmax unchanged (still 100 micromol/min) but raises the apparent Km (2.0 to 6.0 mM), and excess substrate fully overcomes it. That pattern, plus a shared y-intercept (1/Vmax) on the Lineweaver-Burk plot, is the signature of a competitive inhibitor. Pure noncompetitive inhibition would lower Vmax with unchanged Km (that is Inhibitor B). Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Km and Vmax. An irreversible inhibitor could not be reversed by adding substrate. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-2
passages.body:
A biochemistry lab studied how a small globular enzyme, RibN, loses activity when it unfolds. In its native state, RibN is stabilized by a hydrophobic core, numerous hydrogen bonds within its alpha-helices and beta-sheets, and a single disulfide bond linking two cysteine residues. The team monitored folding both by measuring enzyme activity and by tracking buried tryptophan residues, which fluoresce differently when the protein unfolds. Slowly heating the wild-type enzyme, they found that activity was retained up to about 55 deg C and then fell sharply, with a melting temperature (Tm, the temperature at which half the protein is unfolded) of 65 deg C.
They compared three samples. A cysteine-to-alanine mutant that cannot form the disulfide bond behaved like wild type at low temperature but had a Tm of only 52 deg C. Adding 6 M urea, a chemical denaturant, to wild-type enzyme lowered its Tm dramatically and abolished activity even at room temperature; on dialysis to remove the urea, activity slowly returned. Boiling followed by cooling left the protein inactive and aggregated, yet sequencing showed that the polypeptide's amino acid sequence was fully intact.
The investigators emphasized that all of these treatments disrupted the folded shape without breaking the peptide bonds of the backbone, and that the enzyme's function depended on maintaining its three-dimensional conformation, not merely on possessing the correct sequence.

questions.stem: The amino acid sequence that sequencing showed to be intact after boiling corresponds to which level of protein structure?
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the covalently bonded sequence of amino acids; the peptide bonds that define it are not broken by heat, which is why sequencing still reads the full sequence. Secondary (helices/sheets), tertiary (overall 3D fold), and quaternary (subunit assembly) structures all rely on noncovalent interactions that heat disrupts. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-3
passages.body:
To dissect how mutations disrupt protein output, a lab engineered a set of Escherichia coli strains, each carrying a single defined change in a gene (galK) that encodes a metabolic enzyme. For every strain they measured two quantities: the steady-state level of galK messenger RNA (by quantitative PCR) and the amount of functional enzyme (by an activity assay). Results were expressed as a percentage of the wild-type value.
Wild type showed 100 percent mRNA and 100 percent enzyme activity. Strain 1, carrying a substitution in the promoter region upstream of the coding sequence, showed 15 percent mRNA and 14 percent activity. Strain 2, carrying a single base-pair change that converted a glutamine codon (CAG) into a stop codon (TAG) near the beginning of the coding sequence, showed 95 percent mRNA but less than 2 percent activity; the protein it produced was abnormally short. Strain 3, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion just after the start codon, showed 92 percent mRNA and less than 2 percent activity, and its protein product bore no resemblance to the wild-type sequence beyond its first few residues. Strain 4, carrying a base change that altered a codon from CTG to CTA (both of which encode leucine), showed 98 percent mRNA and 97 percent activity.
The investigators noted that a mutation's consequences depend on where in the gene it falls and how it interacts with the genetic code: some changes reduce how much mRNA is made, others corrupt translation of the message, and some have essentially no effect at all.

questions.stem: Strain 1 shows low mRNA (15 percent) with activity (14 percent) that tracks the mRNA level. This points to a defect in:
questions.explanation: A promoter is where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription; a promoter mutation lowers how much mRNA is made. Because activity falls in proportion to mRNA (each mRNA is translated normally), the lesion is at transcription, not translation, folding, or replication. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-4
passages.body:
In a classic-style linkage experiment, geneticists studied two genes in a fruit fly stock: one affecting body color (B = gray, dominant; b = black) and one affecting wing shape (V = normal, dominant; v = vestigial). The two genes reside on the same chromosome. Females heterozygous for both genes, with both dominant alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other (arrangement B V / b v), were testcrossed to males that were homozygous recessive (b v / b v). Because the testcross father contributes only b and v alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reveals which allele combination it received from the mother.
Among 1,000 offspring, the researchers counted four phenotypic classes: 425 gray, normal-winged; 415 black, vestigial-winged; 82 gray, vestigial-winged; and 78 black, normal-winged. The first two classes matched the parental (non-recombinant) allele combinations, whereas the last two classes represented new combinations that could only arise if the maternal homologs exchanged segments.
The team used the frequency of these new-combination offspring to estimate how far apart the two genes lie, applying the rule that one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to a 1 percent recombination frequency. They noted that if the two genes had been on different chromosomes, or extremely far apart on the same one, the four classes would instead have appeared in roughly equal numbers.

questions.stem: Which offspring are the recombinant (new-combination) classes?
questions.explanation: The mother's homologs carried B V and b v, so offspring showing gray-normal or black-vestigial are parental types (the two most frequent classes). The rare gray-vestigial (82) and black-normal (78) offspring carry new allele combinations (B v and b V) produced by crossing over, so they are the recombinants. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-5
passages.body:
To probe how mitochondria couple fuel oxidation to ATP synthesis, researchers suspended isolated mitochondria in a buffered chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, so that the rate of oxygen consumption could be followed continuously. Because the electron transport chain uses O2 as its final electron acceptor, oxygen consumption serves as a readout of electron flow.
The team added an oxidizable substrate (to feed electrons into the chain) plus ADP and inorganic phosphate (the raw materials for ATP synthesis). Oxygen consumption rose to a brisk, steady rate, and ATP accumulated in the chamber. They then added oligomycin, a compound that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Oxygen consumption fell almost to zero, and ATP synthesis stopped. Finally, they added 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a small molecule that ferries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen consumption surged back to a high rate, yet no ATP was produced; the released energy instead appeared as heat.
The investigators explained the pattern in terms of the proton-motive force. Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase normally lets those protons flow back into the matrix, harnessing the gradient to make ATP. Blocking ATP synthase lets the gradient build until it opposes further pumping, so electron flow (and O2 use) slows. A protonophore like DNP short-circuits the gradient, so electron transport races ahead while its energy is dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP.

questions.explanation: At the end of the electron transport chain, O2 accepts the electrons (and protons) to form water; therefore, the rate at which O2 is consumed reflects the rate of electron flow. O2 is not pumped, does not phosphorylate ADP (ATP synthase does that), and does not inhibit ATP synthase. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-6
passages.body:
A cell-biology group compared how three different solutes cross the plasma membrane of cultured cells. For each solute they measured the initial rate of uptake into the cell as a function of the solute's external concentration, under conditions where metabolic ATP could be depleted with an inhibitor when desired.
Solute X, a small hydrophobic steroid, entered at a rate that increased linearly with external concentration and did not plateau even at very high concentrations; depleting ATP had no effect on its uptake. Solute Y, a polar sugar, entered at a rate that rose with concentration and then leveled off at a maximum, tracing a curve resembling enzyme saturation; adding a structurally similar sugar reduced Y's uptake, but ATP depletion did not. Solute Z, an ion, was accumulated inside the cell to a concentration far higher than outside, against its concentration gradient; this uptake collapsed when ATP was depleted.
The researchers interpreted the linear, nonsaturable, ATP-independent uptake of X as simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer. The saturable, competable, but ATP-independent uptake of Y indicated a finite number of specific membrane transport proteins moving the sugar down its gradient. The accumulation of Z against its gradient, abolished by ATP depletion, indicated a pump doing work at the expense of cellular energy. The experiment thus separated three transport modes using two simple criteria: whether the rate saturates, and whether it requires cellular energy.

questions.explanation: Saturation (a maximum rate) and inhibition by a similar sugar indicate a limited number of specific transport proteins, while ATP independence and movement down the gradient make it facilitated diffusion, not active transport. Simple diffusion would not saturate, and osmosis refers to water movement, not sugar. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-7
passages.body:
Microbiologists grew a pure culture of a rod-shaped bacterium in a closed flask of nutrient broth held at 37 deg C and tracked population size by measuring turbidity (optical density) over time. The resulting growth curve had four phases. During an initial lag phase, cell number changed little as the cells synthesized enzymes and adjusted to the medium. This was followed by an exponential (log) phase, during which the population doubled at a constant interval; the team measured a doubling time of 20 minutes. Growth then slowed into a stationary phase, in which the number of new cells produced roughly equaled the number dying, as nutrients ran low and wastes accumulated. Finally, in the death phase, viable counts declined.
To test antibiotics, the researchers exposed separate exponential-phase cultures to two drugs. Penicillin, which blocks the cross-linking step in synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall, killed rapidly growing cells but had little effect on cells that were not actively dividing. A second drug bound the bacterial ribosome and halted protein synthesis, stopping growth without immediately lysing the cells.
The team highlighted features that distinguish these prokaryotes from the animal cells in a companion culture: the bacteria lacked a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, divided asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis, and could acquire new genes horizontally, for example by taking up plasmids during conjugation. These traits shape both how the population grows and how drugs can target the bacteria selectively.

questions.explanation: In 120 minutes there are 120/20 = 6 doublings, so the population multiplies by 2^6 = 64: 1,000 x 64 = 64,000. The other choices assume far fewer doublings or simple addition rather than exponential growth. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-8
passages.body:
A cancer-biology lab used flow cytometry to measure the DNA content of individual cells in a proliferating culture. A fluorescent dye that binds DNA in proportion to its amount let the instrument sort cells by how much DNA each contained. Cells in G1 phase, before DNA replication, showed a baseline amount of DNA (call it 2n). Cells in S phase, actively replicating, showed intermediate amounts between 2n and 4n. Cells in G2 and M, having completed replication, showed 4n. A normal asynchronous culture therefore produced two peaks (at 2n and 4n) with cells spread in between.
The team then treated cells with Drug Q. Afterward, nearly all cells piled up in the 2n peak, with almost none at 4n, indicating an arrest before DNA replication began. In a separate experiment, they examined a cell line carrying a nonfunctional version of a checkpoint protein that normally halts cells with damaged DNA. When these mutant cells were irradiated to damage their DNA, they continued through the cycle and divided anyway, accumulating chromosomal abnormalities over successive generations. Unlike normal cells, the mutant cells also kept dividing after covering the surface of the culture dish, having lost contact inhibition.
The investigators connected these observations to tumor formation: checkpoints normally verify that conditions are correct before a cell commits to replication and division, and loss of these controls allows damaged cells to proliferate, a hallmark of cancer.

G1 cells sit at 2n, cells that exit the cycle (G0) are still 2n, and no phase halves the DNA content except the division into daughter cells. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-9
passages.body:
Neurophysiologists used a squid giant axon and fine electrodes to record the membrane potential during a nerve impulse. At rest, the inside of the axon measured about -70 mV relative to the outside. A brief electrical stimulus that depolarized the membrane to a threshold near -55 mV triggered an all-or-none action potential: the potential shot upward to about +30 mV (the rising phase) and then rapidly returned toward rest (the falling phase), briefly overshooting to a value more negative than -70 mV before stabilizing.
The team dissected the ionic basis using two toxins. Applying tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, abolished the action potential entirely: stimulation no longer produced the rapid upstroke. Applying tetraethylammonium (TEA), which blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, left the upstroke intact but markedly slowed the return to rest, prolonging the action potential. Blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase with a separate agent did not abolish individual action potentials over the short term but, over many impulses, degraded the ion gradients on which they depend.
In a final experiment the researchers compared conduction along a myelinated axon with an unmyelinated one of similar diameter. The myelinated axon conducted impulses far faster, because the action potential regenerated only at the gaps in the myelin (nodes of Ranvier), jumping from node to node. The results tied each phase of the action potential to specific ion channels and showed how myelination speeds signaling without changing the underlying ionic mechanism.

choices.text: sodium influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels

questions.explanation: TTX specifically blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; because blocking them removes the upstroke, the rapid depolarization must be caused by Na+ rushing into the cell through those channels. Potassium efflux drives repolarization (the falling phase), chloride is not the depolarizing current here, and the Na+/K+ ATPase sets up gradients rather than generating the spike. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-10
passages.body:
To study how blood delivers oxygen, physiologists measured the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with O2 across a range of oxygen partial pressures (PO2), generating an oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. For adult hemoglobin the curve was S-shaped (sigmoidal): saturation rose slowly at very low PO2, steeply through intermediate values, and leveled off near 100 percent at high PO2. The partial pressure at which hemoglobin is 50 percent saturated (the P50) was about 26 mmHg. For comparison, myoglobin, a single-subunit muscle protein, gave a hyperbolic curve that was left-shifted, reaching high saturation at much lower PO2.
The team then altered the conditions around adult hemoglobin. Lowering the pH (more acidic), raising the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and raising temperature each shifted the curve to the right, increasing the P50; at any given intermediate PO2, hemoglobin then held less oxygen and released more. These effects are collectively called the Bohr effect. Conversely, fetal hemoglobin gave a left-shifted curve with a lower P50 than adult hemoglobin.
The investigators related the findings to physiology. The sigmoidal shape reflects cooperative binding among hemoglobin's four subunits: O2 binding to one subunit increases the affinity of the others. In metabolically active tissue, where CO2 and acid are high and temperature is elevated, the right shift promotes oxygen unloading exactly where it is needed. The left-shifted fetal curve lets fetal blood extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

has lower O2 affinity and unloads more oxygen to the tissue
can no longer bind oxygen at all

questions.explanation: A higher P50 means more PO2 is needed to reach 50 percent saturation, i.e., lower affinity; at a given PO2 the hemoglobin is less saturated and releases more O2 to the tissue. It does not indicate higher affinity, a total loss of binding, or a change of protein identity. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-bb-11
passages.body:
To characterize kidney function, a renal-physiology team infused test substances into volunteers and measured how the kidneys handled each, using the concept of clearance: the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. They relied on three markers.
Inulin, a plant polysaccharide, is freely filtered at the glomerulus but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules. Its clearance therefore equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which averaged 125 mL/min in the study. Para-aminohippurate (PAH) is both filtered and actively secreted into the tubule, so nearly all PAH is removed in a single pass; its clearance (about 600 mL/min) approximated the renal plasma flow, a value much larger than GFR. Glucose, by contrast, is freely filtered but then almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by carrier proteins; at normal plasma glucose levels its clearance was essentially zero, and none appeared in the urine.
The team then raised plasma glucose experimentally. Below a threshold, urine remained glucose-free. Above the threshold, the reabsorptive carriers became saturated (their transport maximum, or Tm, was exceeded), and glucose spilled into the urine. Because the unreabsorbed glucose held water osmotically within the tubule, urine volume also rose.
The investigators noted that comparing a substance's clearance with the inulin clearance reveals its tubular handling: a clearance below GFR implies net reabsorption, a clearance above GFR implies net secretion, and a clearance equal to GFR implies filtration only.

passages.title: psg-bb-12
passages.body: The following items are discrete (standalone) questions, like the freestanding questions interspersed between passages on the Biological and Biochemical Foundations section of the exam. Each item is self-contained and does not depend on a shared passage; together they sample foundational-concept content across biomolecules, genetics, metabolism, cell division, and physiological coordination. Answer each on the basis of your own content knowledge, using quantitative reasoning where an item supplies data. The grounding sources are the same free, openly licensed textbooks used for the passage sets in this file.

passages.title: psg-cp-1
passages.body:
A biomechanics laboratory studies vertical jumping with a force platform, a rigid plate that records the force a person exerts on it as a function of time. A 60 kg athlete stands motionless on the platform and then performs a maximal jump: she dips down, drives upward, and leaves the plate. High-speed video tracks a marker on her hip to follow the vertical motion of her center of mass.
While the athlete stands still, the platform reads a steady value equal to her weight. During the propulsion phase the reading rises well above this baseline, climbs to a peak, and then drops abruptly to zero at the instant her feet leave the plate. The interval from the start of propulsion to takeoff lasts about 0.20 s. After takeoff the center of mass rises to a measured peak height of 0.45 m above its takeoff position before falling back. Treating the body as a point mass at the center of mass and neglecting air resistance, the researchers reconstruct the takeoff velocity, the mechanical energy of the jump, and the forces during landing.
On landing, the athlete returns to the plate moving downward, and the platform again registers a large force as she decelerates to rest over about 0.15 s. The researchers note that athletes who land with stiff legs stop in a shorter time and record much larger peak forces than athletes who flex their knees and ankles to cushion the impact. Throughout, the platform measures the contact force between athlete and plate; gravitational acceleration is taken as g = 10 m/s^2.

questions.stem: Using the measured peak height of 0.45 m, what was the athlete's vertical speed at the instant of takeoff?
questions.explanation: At the peak the vertical velocity is zero, so v^2 = v0^2 - 2gh gives v0 = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2*10*0.45) = sqrt(9) = 3 m/s. '1.5 m/s' halves the correct value; '9 m/s' reports v0^2 (units m^2/s^2), not v0; '4.5 m/s' comes from incorrectly using v0 = g*h. Only 3 m/s is consistent with a 0.45 m peak height. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

'135 J' drops the factor from mis-halving; '540 J' doubles it; '27 J' omits g. The equality of the KE and PE routes confirms 270 J. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. passages.title: psg-cp-2
passages.body:
Atherosclerotic plaque narrows an artery and changes how blood moves through it. In a benchtop model of a coronary artery, a pump drives an incompressible fluid with the density of blood (1050 kg/m^3) through a rigid tube at a steady volume flow rate. Midway along the tube a molded plaque reduces the internal radius to half its normal value over a short segment before the tube widens again. Pressure sensors record the fluid's lateral (static) pressure against the wall upstream of, within, and downstream of the narrowing, while a Doppler probe measures flow speed at the same locations.
Away from the narrowing the fluid moves at 0.20 m/s. Because the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the same volume per second must cross every section, so the fluid accelerates as it enters the constricted segment. The investigators also compare the pump pressure needed to maintain the flow rate before and after the plaque forms, and they note that the vessel's resistance is extremely sensitive to its radius.
A second module models gas exchange. Air in an alveolus is held at an oxygen partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, while blood entering the surrounding pulmonary capillary has an oxygen partial pressure of about 40 mmHg. A thin, moist membrane separates the two compartments, and the team measures how quickly oxygen crosses as they vary the partial-pressure difference, the membrane thickness, and its area. Height differences in the standing circulation are represented by raising or lowering the capillary bed relative to the pump. Take g = 10 m/s^2.

questions.stem: In the constricted segment, where the radius is half its normal value, what is the flow speed of the blood-mimicking fluid?
questions.explanation: Continuity for an incompressible fluid is A1v1 = A2v2. Halving the radius quarters the cross-sectional area (A ~ r^2), so the speed must quadruple: v2 = 0.20 * 4 = 0.80 m/s. '0.40 m/s' assumes speed scales with 1/r (factor 2); '1.6 m/s' uses factor 8; '0.050 m/s' has the fluid slowing, which violates continuity. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

'4x' uses r^2 (area) scaling; '2x' uses r^1; '8x' uses r^3. The fourth-power dependence is why small radius changes dominate vascular resistance. passages.title: psg-cp-3
passages.body:
Students build and analyze a galvanic (voltaic) cell and then use batteries to study simple circuits. In the cell, a strip of zinc metal sits in zinc sulfate solution and a strip of copper metal sits in copper sulfate solution; a salt bridge connects the two half-cells, and a wire with a voltmeter links the metal strips. Under standard conditions the tabulated reduction potentials are Zn^2+ + 2 e- -> Zn, E = -0.76 V, and Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu, E = +0.34 V. When the wire is connected, one electrode gains mass while the other slowly dissolves, and the voltmeter registers a steady potential difference. The students confirm which metal is oxidized by weighing the electrodes before and after.
They then replace the standard 1 M solutions with more dilute ones and record how the measured cell voltage shifts away from its standard value, relating the change to the reaction quotient Q for Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu.
In the circuit module, a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor wired in parallel with each other, and that combination wired in series with a 4 ohm resistor. An ammeter reads the current leaving the battery. The students compute the equivalent resistance, the current, and the power the battery delivers, treating the battery as an ideal source with negligible internal resistance and the wires as resistanceless.

questions.stem: What is the standard cell potential (EMF) of the zinc-copper cell?
questions.explanation: The cathode is the half-cell with the more positive reduction potential (Cu, +0.34 V); the anode is Zn (-0.76 V). E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V. '0.42 V' subtracts the wrong way in magnitude; '-1.10 V' assigns the electrodes backwards (a nonspontaneous sign); '0.34 V' ignores the zinc half-cell. A positive EMF confirms the reaction is spontaneous as written. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-4
passages.body:
Diagnostic imaging often relies on how waves interact with tissue. In an ultrasound scanner, a transducer emits pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes returning from boundaries between tissues. A common obstetric probe operates at 2.0 MHz, and sound travels through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s. The scanner forms an image from the time delay and strength of each returning echo, and clinicians choose the probe frequency to trade off image detail against how deep the sound can penetrate.
A Doppler mode measures blood flow. When a pulse reflects from red blood cells moving relative to the transducer, the returning sound is shifted in frequency; the scanner converts this shift into a flow velocity and direction, coloring flow toward and away from the probe differently.
A second instrument, a fiber-optic endoscope, guides visible light instead of sound. Light travels along a thin glass fiber whose core has a higher refractive index (about 1.5) than its surrounding cladding (about 1.2). Rays that strike the core-cladding boundary at a large enough angle are trapped inside the core and travel the fiber's length with little loss, so the endoscope can illuminate and image tissue deep inside the body and around bends. The physicians rely on the same refraction principles when a laser beam crosses from one tissue layer into another and changes direction. Throughout, the team treats soft tissue as a uniform medium for sound and the fiber as an ideal light guide.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of the 2.0 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue (speed 1540 m/s)?
questions.explanation: The wave relation v = f*lambda gives lambda = v/f = 1540/(2.0x10^6) = 7.7x10^-4 m = 0.77 mm. '7.7 mm' is off by 10x; '0.077 mm' by 10x the other way; '1.3 mm' inverts a step. Sub-millimeter wavelength is why ultrasound can resolve fine structures. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-5
passages.body:
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive isotopes to image the body. The most widely used tracer, technetium-99m, is a metastable ('m') nuclear state that returns to its ground state by emitting a single gamma-ray photon, without changing its number of protons or neutrons. Because those gamma photons escape the body and reach a gamma camera, and because the isotope's half-life is a convenient 6.0 hours, it images well and clears quickly. A patient receives an initial activity of 800 MBq, and the staff track how the activity falls over the following day.
Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a different decay. Fluorine-18, built into a glucose analog, decays by positron emission: inside the nucleus a proton is converted into a neutron, and a positron is ejected. The positron soon annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two photons the scanner detects in coincidence.
The passage also compares decay modes. Some heavy parents decay by alpha emission, ejecting a helium-4 nucleus, while others undergo beta-minus decay. In every case the totals of mass number and charge are conserved across the nuclear equation. Finally, the team notes that alpha, beta, and especially gamma emissions are all 'ionizing': each quantum can carry enough energy to eject electrons from the atoms it strikes, which is both the basis of detection and the reason for strict dose limits. Planck's relation ties a photon's energy to its frequency, and gamma photons lie at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.stem: Technetium-99m has a 6.0 hour half-life. If the patient starts with 800 MBq, what activity remains 24 hours later (ignoring biological clearance)?
questions.explanation: In 24 hours there are 24/6 = 4 half-lives, so the surviving fraction is (1/2)^4 = 1/16, giving 800/16 = 50 MBq. '100 MBq' uses 3 half-lives; '200 MBq' uses 2; '25 MBq' uses 5. Each half-life halves the activity: 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 -> 50. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-6
passages.body:
Water's ability to dissolve ions and to resist changes in acidity underlies much of physiology. Blood plasma is held near pH 7.4 largely by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer: dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-. The effective pKa for this equilibrium in plasma is about 6.1. Normally the concentration of bicarbonate is roughly twenty times that of dissolved carbonic acid, and the lungs and kidneys adjust the two components to hold that ratio steady. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links the pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
To study buffering directly, students titrate a weak acid at 25 C. They place 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.74) in a flask and add sodium hydroxide from a burette while a pH meter records the curve. Early on the pH rises slowly through a buffering plateau; near the end it climbs steeply through the equivalence point, where exactly enough base has been added to neutralize all the acid. A separate reference solution at 25 C is measured to have a pH of 3.0.
The students note that at 25 C the ion product of water fixes pH + pOH = 14, and that a solution's acidity reflects the balance between hydrogen and hydroxide ions produced when water and solutes interact. They also test the buffer's resilience by adding a few drops of strong acid to the bicarbonate system and to plain water, comparing how far the pH of each moves.

questions.stem: Using pKa = 6.1 and a bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio of 20:1, what blood pH does the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation predict?
questions.explanation: pH = pKa + log([HCO3-]/[H2CO3]) = 6.1 + log(20) = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.4. '6.1' forgets the ratio term (log 1 = 0); '4.8' subtracts instead of adds; '8.7' uses log(400). The 20:1 ratio is exactly what places physiological pH at 7.4 despite a pKa of 6.1. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-7
passages.body:
The physical properties of a substance are set largely by the forces between its molecules. Consider a data set the students assemble. Among the hydrides of Group 16, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) boils at -60 C, yet water (H2O), a lighter molecule, boils at +100 C - a striking exception to the usual trend that heavier molecules boil higher. The students also compare two compounds with the identical formula C2H6O: ethanol, which boils at 78 C, and dimethyl ether, which boils at -24 C. Finally, they tabulate the boiling points of the noble gases and find a steady rise from helium through xenon.
To interpret the data they review molecular structure. Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so each O-H bond is polar; in water the two O-H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen arrange the electron domains tetrahedrally, giving the molecule a bent shape with an H-O-H angle near 104.5 degrees and a net dipole moment. They classify the intermolecular forces available to each substance: London dispersion forces (present in all molecules, stronger in larger and more polarizable electron clouds), dipole-dipole forces (between permanent dipoles), and hydrogen bonding (the especially strong attraction when H bonded to N, O, or F is drawn to a lone pair on another such atom).
Their goal is to connect each measured boiling point to the strongest intermolecular force a molecule can form, and to explain the anomalies - water's high boiling point, ethanol versus its isomer, and the noble-gas trend - in terms of hydrogen bonding, polarity, geometry, and polarizability.

questions.stem: Why does water boil at 100 C while the heavier H2S boils at -60 C?

choices.text: Water forms hydrogen bonds (O-H to a lone pair on another O), which are far stronger than the dispersion/dipole forces available to H2S.
Water is nonpolar, so its molecules pack more tightly than those of H2S.
H2S is a larger molecule, so it has weaker dispersion forces than water.
Water has a lower molar mass, and lighter molecules always boil higher.

questions.explanation: Sulfur is not electronegative enough to support strong hydrogen bonding, so H2S is held together mainly by weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces; water's extensive O-H...O hydrogen bonding makes it boil far higher despite its lower mass. Choice 2 wrongly calls water nonpolar; choice 3 has the dispersion comparison backwards; choice 4 states a false general rule. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-8
passages.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

questions.stem: The spot traveled 3.0 cm and the solvent front advanced 5.0 cm. What is the spot's Rf?
questions.explanation: Rf = (distance traveled by the compound)/(distance traveled by the solvent front) = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. '1.67' inverts the ratio; '0.30' and '0.15' come from dividing by the wrong distance. Rf is dimensionless and always between 0 and 1. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cp-9
passages.body:
Nucleophilic substitution is central to organic and biochemical reactivity, from laboratory synthesis to the alkylation of DNA. A class studies how two bromoalkanes react with hydroxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile, in a hydroxylic solvent.
The first substrate is 1-bromobutane, a primary alkyl halide in which the carbon bearing bromine is attached to only one other carbon. With a good nucleophile it reacts by a one-step, concerted mechanism (SN2): hydroxide attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving bromide, and as bromide departs the other three groups invert like an umbrella in the wind. The measured rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the hydroxide.
The second substrate is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), a tertiary halide whose brominated carbon is attached to three other carbons. It reacts by a two-step mechanism (SN1): the carbon-bromine bond breaks first to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. The measured rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, and because the carbocation is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can approach from either face.
The class also revisits structure. They note that a carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocenter and examine 2-bromobutane as an example. They track how the functional group changes when hydroxide replaces bromide, and they rank the stability of primary, secondary, and tertiary carbocations to explain why substrate structure dictates the mechanism. passages.title: psg-cp-10
passages.body:
A research team studies both how fast a reaction goes and whether it goes at all - kinetics and thermodynamics, two independent questions. They first examine the decomposition of a reactant, X, measuring its initial rate as they vary the starting concentration at fixed temperature. In three trials the initial concentration of X is 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 M, and the corresponding initial rates are 2.0x10^-3, 8.0x10^-3, and 1.8x10^-2 M/s. From these data they extract the reaction order in X and the rate constant.
They then vary temperature and find, as expected, that the rate rises steeply as the sample is warmed. They interpret this with the Arrhenius picture: only molecules with at least the activation energy can react, and warming increases that fraction. Adding a catalyst speeds the reaction further, and the team is careful to note what a catalyst does and does not change.
Separately, they assess the reaction's thermodynamics. Calorimetry gives a standard enthalpy change delta_H = +50 kJ/mol, and the standard entropy change is delta_S = +100 J/(mol.K). Using the Gibbs relation delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S, they compute the free-energy change at 298 K to judge spontaneity, and they determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous. They stress that kinetics (how fast) and thermodynamics (how favorable) are separate: a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet immeasurably slow, or fast yet unfavorable. They treat delta_H and delta_S as approximately constant over the range considered.

questions.stem: Based on the initial-rate data, what is the reaction order with respect to X?
questions.explanation: Going from 0.10 to 0.20 M doubles [X], and the rate rises from 2.0x10^-3 to 8.0x10^-3 M/s - a factor of 4. Since rate ~ [X]^n and 2^n = 4, n = 2 (second order). The 0.30 M trial confirms it: tripling [X] gives 9x the rate (1.8x10^-2). Zero, first, and third order predict 1x, 2x, and 8x, respectively. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

questions.stem: A forearm holds a 50 N ball in the hand, 30 cm from the elbow joint, while the biceps tendon attaches 3.0 cm from the elbow. Ignoring the forearm's weight, what muscle force keeps the forearm horizontal and in static equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Rotational equilibrium about the elbow requires the muscle torque to balance the load torque: F_m x 0.030 m = 50 N x 0.30 m, so F_m = (50 x 0.30)/0.030 = 500 N. The short lever arm of the muscle forces a large force (a class-3 lever trades force for range of motion). '50 N' ignores the lever arms; '150 N' uses a factor of 3 only; '5000 N' misplaces a decimal. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-1
passages.body:
Researchers investigated how listeners detect faint tones and how expectations shape perception. In Experiment 1, 40 young adults sat in a soundproof booth and reported whether a brief 1000-Hz tone was present on each of 400 trials. The tone was actually presented on only half of the trials; on the rest, participants heard only background noise. Investigators varied the tone's intensity to estimate each listener's absolute threshold, defined as the intensity detected on 50% of trials. They also recorded four response categories - hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections - and computed a sensitivity index (d') separately from each listener's response criterion.
In Experiment 2, the same listeners were told before each block whether tones would be 'rare' or 'common.' When told tones were common, listeners reported hearing a tone more often, producing more hits but also more false alarms, even though the physical stimuli were identical across blocks. Sensitivity (d') did not change between the 'rare' and 'common' blocks; only the criterion shifted.
In Experiment 3, listeners judged whether two successive weights differed. The smallest detectable difference grew in proportion to the starting weight: distinguishing 102 g from 100 g was as hard as distinguishing 204 g from 200 g. Finally, when a steady tone played continuously, listeners' reported loudness declined over several minutes, though an abrupt change in intensity was noticed at once. The authors concluded that detection reflects both sensory capacity and decision processes, and that the sensory system is tuned to change rather than to constant stimulation.

questions.stem: The intensity 'detected on 50% of trials' corresponds to which concept?
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity an observer can detect 50% of the time - exactly the definition used in Experiment 1. A difference threshold (just-noticeable difference) is about telling two stimuli apart, not detecting one against no stimulus. Weber's constant is the fixed ratio behind the difference threshold, and the response criterion is a decision variable, not a sensory limit. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-2
passages.body:
A memory researcher tested how the way information is studied affects later recall. In Phase 1, 90 undergraduates saw a list of 30 common nouns, one every three seconds. Each word was preceded by one of three questions: whether the word was printed in capital letters (structural), whether it rhymed with a target word (phonemic), or whether it fit meaningfully into a sentence (semantic). After a filled delay, participants took a surprise free-recall test.
Recall rose steadily with the depth of processing: 18% for structural, 37% for phonemic, and 65% for semantic judgments. In addition, regardless of the processing condition, words from the beginning and end of the list were recalled better than words from the middle. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds of counting backward, the advantage for the last few items disappeared, but the advantage for the first few items remained.
In Phase 2, participants watched a short video of a car approaching an intersection. Afterward, half were asked, 'How fast was the car going when it passed the yield sign?' though the video actually showed a stop sign. A week later, participants who had received the misleading question were far more likely to report having seen a yield sign than participants asked a neutral question. passages.title: psg-ps-3
passages.body:
Investigators examined how bodily arousal and its interpretation combine to produce emotion. In Study 1, 120 volunteers received an injection described as a vitamin; half actually received a mild dose of adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and produces jitteriness, and half received saline. Within each group, some were accurately told to expect arousal symptoms and others were told nothing. Each participant then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or irritated. Aroused participants who had not been warned about the symptoms reported emotions matching the confederate's mood - euphoria or anger - more strongly than warned participants or saline controls. Participants who could attribute their arousal to the injection were less swayed by the confederate.
In Study 2, the same volunteers completed a stressful mental-arithmetic task while salivary cortisol was sampled. Cortisol rose within 20 minutes, peaked, and then declined once the task ended. Participants who appraised the task as a 'challenge' showed a smaller cortisol response than those who appraised it as a 'threat,' despite identical task difficulty. Reported stress correlated with threat appraisal, not with objective performance.
The authors linked Study 1 to a theory holding that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal, and linked Study 2 to a model in which the same stressor produces different physiological responses depending on how it is appraised. They noted that the cortisol time course mirrored the mobilize-then-recover pattern of the body's general response to stressors.

questions.stem: Study 1 - arousal plus the confederate's mood determined the emotion, and an available attribution weakened the effect - best supports:
questions.explanation: Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory holds that emotion requires physiological arousal PLUS a cognitive label drawn from context; unexplained arousal took on the confederate's mood, while participants who blamed the injection had a non-emotional label and felt less. James-Lange ties each emotion to a specific bodily pattern, Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur independently and simultaneously, and facial feedback concerns expressions driving emotion. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-4
passages.body:
A team studied what sustains effort on a task. Ninety children who already enjoyed drawing were randomly assigned to three groups. The 'expected-reward' group was promised a certificate for drawing; the 'unexpected-reward' group drew and then received the same certificate as a surprise; the 'no-reward' group simply drew. Two weeks later, during free-play periods, observers unobtrusively recorded how much each child chose to draw. Children in the expected-reward group spent about half as much free time drawing as the other two groups, whose behavior did not differ.
In a second study with adults, participants worked on solvable puzzles under one of two framings. Some were told the task measured 'innate intelligence'; others were told that effort and strategy drive success. After encountering difficult items, the 'effort' group persisted longer and reported greater interest, and this difference was largest among participants who scored high on a measure of conscientiousness.
The researchers interpreted the children's result as evidence that offering an expected tangible reward for an already-enjoyable activity can reduce later voluntary engagement, because the behavior becomes attributed to the external incentive. They connected the adult result to a framework distinguishing motivation that arises from within the person from motivation driven by external consequences, and noted that a stable personality dimension moderated persistence. They cautioned that rewards are not universally harmful: unexpected rewards, and rewards for dull tasks, did not undermine engagement.

questions.stem: The expected-reward group's reduced later drawing best illustrates:
questions.explanation: The overjustification effect occurs when an expected external reward for an already-intrinsically-enjoyable activity undermines later intrinsic motivation - here, halving voluntary drawing. Negative and secondary reinforcement would increase behavior, and learned helplessness follows uncontrollable aversive events, neither of which applies. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-5
passages.body:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.
In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.
In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.
The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

Informational influence is conforming because you believe the group is more accurate; obedience involves orders from an authority; and group polarization is discussion making views more extreme. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-6
passages.body:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).
Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.
In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.
The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

questions.stem: High-relevance readers' reliance on argument strength reflects which route of the elaboration likelihood model?
questions.explanation: In the elaboration likelihood model, motivated (here, high-relevance) recipients take the central route, effortfully evaluating argument quality. The peripheral route relies on surface cues such as source prestige. Classical conditioning and mere exposure are different attitude-formation mechanisms. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-7
passages.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

questions.explanation: Bandura's self-efficacy is the belief in one's capability to succeed at specific tasks, which predicts effort and persistence - as observed. Self-esteem is global self-worth, locus of control is the second construct in the study, and the self-serving bias is an attribution pattern. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-8
passages.body:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.
In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.
The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

choices.text: A genuine ability difference between groups

questions.explanation: Stereotype threat is the fear of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which can depress performance independent of ability - hence the gap appears only when the test is framed as diagnostic of ability. A true ability difference would appear in both conditions; mere exposure and deindividuation are unrelated. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-9
passages.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

questions.stem: Describing medicine as 'an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles' reflects which paradigm, and connects to whose 'sick role' concept?
questions.explanation: Framing an institution by how it preserves social stability is structural functionalism; Parsons's 'sick role' casts illness as a temporary sanctioned role with rights (excused duties) and obligations (seek care). Conflict theory emphasizes power struggles, symbolic interactionism emphasizes meaning, and feminist theory emphasizes gendered structures. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-ps-10
passages.body:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.
Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.
Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

questions.explanation: A step-by-step improvement in health at each higher SES level is the socioeconomic (social) gradient in health. A threshold effect would show a single cutoff, not a gradient; the demographic transition concerns birth/death rates; and the sick role concerns illness behavior. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cars-1
passages.body:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.
Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.
For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.
The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.
It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:

choices.text: show that even an apparently simple object raises a distinction between appearance and reality
demonstrate that the senses cannot be trusted to reveal any truth about the world
argue that painters perceive objects more accurately than ordinary observers do
establish that the real table is uniformly brown, rectangular, and smooth

questions.explanation: The passage opens with a general question about certainty but immediately grounds it in the concrete table in order to develop 'the distinction between appearance and reality' — that development is its purpose (A). (B) overstates the text: the author says confidence 'begins to desert us' and still holds that a real table may be reached by inference, not that the senses reveal no truth. (C) misuses the painter, who is said to see things 'as they appear,' not more truly than they really are. (D) contradicts the passage, which denies the table has any one real colour or texture. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passages.title: psg-cars-2
passages.body:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.
Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.
Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.
Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.
The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.
A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.
